t: Early pregnancy: ectopic, pregnancy loss and trophoblastic disease
sub: Four questions sort early-pregnancy bleeding and pain into normal pregnancy, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or molar disease.

pretest.q: A woman with a positive pregnancy test has a serum hCG of 4,000 mIU/mL and no intrauterine sac on transvaginal ultrasound. What is the main concern?
pretest.why: Above the discriminatory zone, about 3,500 mIU/mL, a normal pregnancy inside the uterus should already show a sac. So an empty uterus means ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise, with a miscarriage that has already passed as the main alternative.

w.Normal early intrauterine pregnancy: At this hCG a normal pregnancy should already show a sac. Not seeing one is reasonable only when hCG is below the discriminatory zone.
w.Complete molar pregnancy: A complete mole fills the uterus with cystic tissue in a snowstorm pattern, so the cavity would not look empty.
w.Threatened abortion: Threatened abortion needs a live pregnancy that is visible inside the uterus, with a closed os. Here no pregnancy has been seen at all.

pretest.q: Which karyotype is typical of a complete hydatidiform mole?
o: 46,XX, one maternal and one paternal set
pretest.why: A complete mole starts with an egg that has lost its own nucleus. One sperm duplicates its DNA, or two sperm fertilize the egg, so every chromosome is paternal. With no maternal genes, no fetus forms.

w.69,XXY, two paternal sets: Triploidy from a normal egg and two sperm is a partial mole. It has fetal parts and a lower hCG.
w.46,XX, one maternal and one paternal set: One maternal and one paternal set is a normal conceptus. A complete mole has lost every maternal chromosome.
w.45,X, maternal: Monosomy X is Turner syndrome, a common chromosomal cause of early pregnancy loss with cystic hygroma. It is not a molar pregnancy.

pretest.q: A woman at 9 weeks has bleeding, a closed cervical os and an embryo with cardiac activity. What is the diagnosis?
pretest.why: Bleeding with a closed os and a live embryo inside the uterus is a threatened abortion. Most of these pregnancies continue, so the usual plan is to wait and watch.

w.Inevitable abortion: In an inevitable abortion the internal os has already opened with the products still inside. Once the cervix dilates, the loss cannot be stopped.
w.Missed abortion: A missed abortion is a nonviable pregnancy with no heartbeat, kept behind a closed os, often with little or no bleeding.
w.Incomplete abortion: In an incomplete abortion some tissue has passed through an open os and some remains, so bleeding and cramping go on.

body: How do you work through bleeding or pain in early pregnancy?

Every patient with bleeding or pain in early pregnancy gets the same four questions, in order. Is she pregnant? A urine or serum **pregnancy test** detects hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin), a hormone made by trophoblast, the cells that form the placenta. It proves trophoblast exists, not where it is. Is the pregnancy inside the uterus? Transvaginal ultrasound answers that. Is it viable, meaning alive and growing? Cardiac activity and a rising hCG show that. Is she stable? Fainting, shoulder pain, severe pain or low blood pressure suggest rupture with internal bleeding, so this check comes first. Pain plus bleeding plus a positive test, with no pregnancy seen in the uterus, is an **ectopic pregnancy** until proven otherwise.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows a normal pregnancy in a set order, timed in the table below. What matters is what each sign proves. A true **gestational sac** has a {{rp26_dds|double decidual sign}}: two bright rings made by the two layers of decidua, the pregnant uterine lining. The pseudosac of an ectopic pregnancy is only fluid in the cavity and has one ring. The **yolk sac** is the first definite proof of a pregnancy inside the uterus. The **fetal pole**, the embryo itself, and then its heartbeat follow.

The hCG level is always read together with the ultrasound. The {{rp26_dz|discriminatory zone}} is the hCG level above which a normal pregnancy should always show a sac, roughly 1,500 to 3,500 mIU/mL. Current guidance leans toward 3,500, so that a wanted pregnancy is never mistaken for an ectopic one. An empty uterus above that level means ectopic pregnancy or a miscarriage that has already passed. Below it, an empty uterus is a {{rp26_pul|pregnancy of unknown location}}. This is sorted out with **serial** hCG levels 48 hours apart plus repeat imaging. In a normal early pregnancy, hCG rises by at least about 35 to 50 percent every 48 hours and often doubles. A failing pregnancy falls, and an ectopic pregnancy often rises slowly or plateaus.
Fluid-filled sac with a double decidual ring
First definite sign of a pregnancy inside the uterus
The embryo itself; its length dates the pregnancy
The embryo is alive; no heartbeat once the crown-rump length is 7 mm or more means loss, and a smaller embryo is rescanned
One hCG value cannot locate a pregnancy

A single hCG proves only that trophoblast exists. Location needs ultrasound, and viability needs a trend over 48 hours. Acting on one number can mean giving methotrexate to a wanted pregnancy, or sending home a woman whose ectopic is still growing. Pain, instability or free fluid on ultrasound override any hCG value.
What else causes first-trimester bleeding, and what about Rh?

About a quarter of pregnant women bleed in the first trimester, and most of those pregnancies continue. Common harmless causes are light implantation spotting near the time of the expected period, and a cervical polyp or fragile cervix that bleeds after intercourse. The serious causes are ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage and molar pregnancy, covered below. Blood type matters too. If fetal red cells reach the blood of an **Rh-negative** woman, she can form anti-D antibodies that harm a later Rh-positive baby. Rh immune globulin prevents this. As of 2025, ACOG's 2024 update lets clinicians forgo Rh testing and Rh immune globulin only after an abortion or pregnancy loss before 12 weeks, whether spontaneous, induced or threatened. It is still given for an ectopic pregnancy (50 mcg before 12 weeks, 300 mcg from 12 weeks) and after molar evacuation. From 12 weeks on, it is given within 72 hours for any loss or bleeding.
Why is ectopic pregnancy the diagnosis you cannot miss?

A fertilized egg normally reaches the uterus and implants about 6 to 7 days after fertilization. Anything that slows its trip through the tube lets it implant there instead. The most common cause is scarring and damaged cilia from **pelvic inflammatory disease**, usually caused by chlamydia. The highest risk comes from a prior ectopic pregnancy or tubal surgery. Other risks are smoking, infertility treatment such as IVF, and pregnancy with an IUD in place. About 1 to 2 percent of pregnancies are ectopic, and most implant in the **ampulla**, the long middle stretch of the tube. The tube cannot stretch like the uterus, so trophoblast eats into its wall and vessels. **Rupture** then causes bleeding into the abdomen (hemoperitoneum), the leading cause of first-trimester maternal death.

The classic picture is a missed period, abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, with a tender adnexal mass, an empty uterus and a slowly rising hCG. Shoulder pain means blood is irritating the diaphragm. Low blood pressure with peritoneal signs means rupture, so an unstable patient goes straight to surgery to remove the tube. A stable patient with an unruptured ectopic, no embryonic heartbeat and a modest hCG can instead get intramuscular **methotrexate**. This folate antagonist blocks dihydrofolate reductase and kills rapidly dividing trophoblast. Her hCG is then followed down to zero.
How do the types of pregnancy loss differ?

Early pregnancy loss ends about 10 to 20 percent of recognized pregnancies. At least half of first-trimester losses come from chromosomal abnormalities in the embryo, mostly autosomal trisomies, and not from exercise, sex or stress. Each type of loss is named from two findings: whether the cervical os (the opening) is open, and whether tissue has passed. A **threatened** abortion has a closed os and a live embryo, so most continue. In an **inevitable** abortion the os has opened and the loss cannot be stopped. A **missed** abortion is a nonviable pregnancy, including an empty sac with no embryo, that stays behind a closed os, often with little or no bleeding. Treatment is waiting, medication (misoprostol, often after mifepristone) or suction.
Nonviable embryo or empty sac retained
Recurrent loss has a short list of causes

Two or more losses call for a search for treatable causes. {{rp26_apls|Antiphospholipid syndrome}} causes clots in the placenta and is treated with low-dose aspirin plus heparin. A **septate uterus** gives the embryo a poorly vascularized place to implant and can be resected. A parent with a **balanced translocation** makes embryos with unbalanced chromosomes, which karyotyping of both partners can find. Uncontrolled diabetes and thyroid disease also cause recurrent loss.
What makes a pregnancy molar, and who is at risk?

A hydatidiform mole is an abnormal conception whose trophoblast overgrows because it carries too many paternal chromosomes. In a **complete mole**, an egg that has lost its own nucleus is fertilized by one sperm, which then duplicates its DNA. Less often, two sperm fertilize it. The result is usually 46,XX with every chromosome **paternal**. With no maternal genes, no embryo forms, and every villus swells into a grape-like vesicle ringed by growing trophoblast. In a **partial mole**, a normal egg is fertilized by two sperm, giving a triploid 69,XXY karyotype. The maternal set lets fetal parts form, but the fetus is abnormal and cannot survive. A mole is more likely at the extremes of maternal age, in teenagers and women over 35, and after a prior mole.
Paternal genes build placenta; maternal genes build the embryo

Genomic imprinting explains the pattern. Paternal genes drive growth of the trophoblast, while maternally expressed genes such as p57 are needed to build the embryo. A complete mole has only paternal chromosomes, so it grows trophoblast but no fetus, and it is negative on the {{rp26_p57|p57 immunostain}}. A partial mole keeps one maternal set, so fetal parts form and the cells stain positive.

Very high hCG produces most of the clinical clues. The patient bleeds or passes grape-like tissue, and her uterus is larger than dates. She may also have **hyperemesis gravidarum** (severe vomiting), preeclampsia before 20 weeks, theca lutein ovarian cysts and sometimes hyperthyroidism. The "why" box below explains how hCG causes these. Ultrasound of a complete mole shows a **snowstorm**, or cluster-of-grapes, pattern with no fetus.

Under the microscope, a complete mole has diffusely swollen ({{rp26_hydropic|hydropic}}) villi with fluid-filled central spaces, ringed by overgrown, atypical trophoblast. It has no fetal tissue or fetal vessels. A partial mole mixes swollen villi with normal-sized ones, has scalloped villous outlines and only focal trophoblast overgrowth, and contains fetal tissue or fetal red cells. The p57 stain separates the two.
Focal cystic placenta with a fetus
Suspected mole, uterus large for dates
How is a molar pregnancy managed, and when does it become cancer?
Managing a molar pregnancy, in order

Baseline tests include hCG, a blood count, blood type with Rh status and thyroid function. Thyroid function matters because hCG can cause hyperthyroidism, and the blood count and blood type matter because a molar uterus can bleed heavily. A chest x-ray looks for spread to the lungs.

Suction curettage empties the uterus and controls the bleeding. Medical evacuation is avoided because it bleeds more and leaves more persistent disease. An Rh-negative woman receives Rh immune globulin.
hCG is checked regularly until it is undetectable and then for several more months, because a mole can persist even after a clean evacuation.
Reliable hormonal contraception keeps a new pregnancy from raising hCG and hiding a recurrence.
Act on a plateau or rise
An hCG that plateaus or rises means trophoblast is persisting, so the patient is staged and referred for chemotherapy.

A **plateau or rise** in hCG after evacuation defines {{rp26_gtn|gestational trophoblastic neoplasia}} (GTN), in which the trophoblast persists and behaves like a tumor. About 15 to 20 percent of complete moles progress, compared with only a few percent of partial moles. GTN can follow any pregnancy. About half of cases follow a mole, and the rest follow a miscarriage, an ectopic pregnancy or a normal term pregnancy.

Tumor cells spread through the blood, so chest imaging looks for metastases, especially in the lungs, where they cause cough, hemoptysis or dyspnea, and the disease is staged and scored for risk. Low-risk disease is cured with single-agent chemotherapy, methotrexate or **actinomycin D**. High-risk disease needs several drugs together. Placental site trophoblastic tumor responds poorly to chemotherapy and is treated by hysterectomy.
Molar villi that invade the myometrium
Local; can perforate the uterus, rarely spreads
Sheets of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, no villi, with hemorrhage
Spreads through blood to lung, vagina, brain and liver; can follow any pregnancy
Intermediate trophoblast of the implantation site
Slow uterine mass, often after a term birth; mostly local

body.q: After evacuation of a complete mole, a woman's hCG falls for 4 weeks and then stays flat for 3 weeks. Which reasoning is best?
o: A plateau is normal laboratory variation, so hCG can be rechecked in 6 months once she stops contraception
A plateau means she has conceived again, so an ultrasound should look for a new intrauterine pregnancy
A plateau means only that some tissue was left behind, so a repeat curettage will always cure her
A plateau means trophoblast is persisting and growing, so it is gestational trophoblastic neoplasia and needs staging and chemotherapy
body.why: After a complete evacuation, hCG should fall steadily to undetectable. A plateau or a rise means trophoblast is surviving and dividing, which defines gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. She needs staging, including a chest x-ray for lung spread, and usually single-agent methotrexate or actinomycin D, which cures most low-risk disease. Contraception during follow-up keeps a new pregnancy from being mistaken for persistent disease. Repeat curettage alone does not reliably treat trophoblast that has invaded the myometrium.

body: Why can a molar pregnancy cause hyperthyroidism and severe vomiting?

Both come from the huge amount of hCG that the overgrown trophoblast makes, often well over 100,000 mIU/mL. hCG shares its alpha subunit with TSH, LH and FSH. Its beta subunit is similar enough to TSH's that, at these levels, hCG activates the TSH receptor. So free T4 rises and TSH falls. The same excess causes hyperemesis gravidarum, whose repeated vomiting leads to weight loss, ketosis and a hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Twin pregnancies also make more hCG, which is why they cause it too. hCG also overstimulates LH receptors in the ovaries, which forms theca lutein cysts. Once the mole is evacuated, hCG falls and all of these problems resolve.

grid.q: Which findings point to a complete hydatidiform mole?
items: Adnexal mass with an empty uterus
hCG rising less than 35 percent in 48 hours
